result:
At closing time, the librarian tipped the book-return bin and heard something roll. It was a lemon, a good one, heavy for its size. She set it on the desk and finished checking in the books.

There was a place in the lost-property drawer for keys, and a place for glasses, and a large and frankly optimistic place for single gloves. There was no place for a lemon. She left it by the date stamp.

At nine the next morning a small boy came in with his father.

“Did you get it?” he asked.

“The lemon?”

He nodded, relieved. His father put a hand on his shoulder. “Tell her why, Cal.”

Cal studied the carpet. “You said I could bring back anything I took out.”

“And you took out a lemon?”

“From the tree in the courtyard.”

She had wondered about that tree. In six years she had seen it produce exactly one lemon, high on a branch above the bench. Apparently all it had needed was another week and a boy with a father tall enough to lift him.

“You can keep it,” she said. “Fruit works differently from books.”

Cal picked up the lemon. It filled both his hands. “What about the seeds?”

“Those you can bring back.”

He did, on Thursday, in an envelope marked LEMON PARTS. By then she had found a pot.
